Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Texas authorities released court documents Thursday detailing the items seized from the medical office and storage unit of Dr. Conrad Murray, the cardiologist who was with Michael Jackson when he fell ill and died on June 25. Dr. Conrad Murray's office was searched Wednesday for "evidence of the offense of manslaughter." Detectives searched both sites in Houston on Wednesday for "evidence of the offense of manslaughter," according to court documents. Murray's attorney confirmed the search Wednesday. Among the items removed from Murray's office were a computer; 27 tablets of Phentermine, a prescription-strength appetite suppressant; 1 tablet of clonazepam, an anti-anxiety medication; and some Rolodex cards. From Murray's storage unit, authorities removed two computer hard drives; an "important contact list"; a suspension notice from Houston's Doctors Hospital; notices from the Internal Revenue Service; and a list of medical and hospital documents. Jackson's former nurse, Cherilyn Lee, was also approached on Wednesday by investigators who wanted copies of medical files she had on the singer, Lee told CNN's Nancy Grace. Lee said she handed over the files to officials with the coroner's office. Ed Chernoff, a Houston lawyer hired by Murray soon after Jackson's death, confirmed that Los Angeles Police detectives and federal Drug Enforcement Administration agents used a search warrant to enter Murray's office in northeast Houston on Wednesday morning. "The search warrant authorized law enforcement to search for and seize items, including documents, they believed constituted evidence of the offense of manslaughter," Chernoff said in a written statement Wednesday. Chernoff said members of Murray's legal team were at the medical office during the search, which he said "was conducted by members of the DEA, two robbery-homicide detectives from the Los Angeles Police Department and Houston Police officers." "Law enforcement concluded their search around 12:30 p.m. and left with a forensic image of a business computer hard drive and 21 documents. None of the documents taken had previously been requested by law enforcement or the L.A. coroner's office," Chernoff said. Tammy Kidd, a spokeswoman at Chernoff's office, said the search "was absolutely a surprise to us, because we've had open lines of communication this whole time." "Based on Dr. Murray's minute-by-minute and item-by-item description of Michael Jackson's last days, he should not be a target of criminal charges," Chernoff said Tuesday. "Dr. Murray was the last doctor standing when Michael Jackson died and it seems all the fury is directed toward him." Los Angeles investigators have interviewed Murray twice, Chernoff said. A third interview has not been scheduled, he said. Police impounded his car, which had been parked at Jackson's Holmby Hills home, the night after Jackson's death. It was released to Murray several days later. "Dr. Murray is frustrated by negative and often erroneous media reports. He has to walk around 24-7 with a bodyguard," Chernoff said. "He can't operate his practice. He can't go to work because he is harassed no matter where he goes." At least two investigations are under way into Jackson's death. The Los Angeles County coroner is waiting for toxicology results to determine a cause of death, while the city Police Department, with assistance from the Drug Enforcement Administration, is looking at the possibility of criminal charges. A coroner's office spokesman said the autopsy findings could be released in the next week or more. Los Angeles Police Chief William Bratton told CNN he would wait for the coroner to determine the exact cause of Jackson's death. "And based on those, we will have an idea of what it is we are dealing (with): Are we dealing with a homicide, or are we dealing with an accidental overdose?" he said. CNN's Alan Duke, Ted Rowlands and Randi Kaye contributed to this report.

(CNN) — Court records made public by Texas officials on Thursday listed property taken from the Houston medical office and storage facility of Dr. Conrad Murray. Murray, a cardiologist, was present when Michael Jackson became ill and died on June 25.

According to the documents, detectives searched both locations Wednesday under a warrant seeking “evidence of the offense of manslaughter.” Murray’s lawyer confirmed the searches that day.

Investigators collected several items from Murray’s office, including a computer, Rolodex cards, 27 Phentermine pills—a prescription-strength drug used to suppress appetite—and one clonazepam tablet, which is used to treat anxiety.

Authorities also seized materials from Murray’s storage unit. Those items included two computer hard drives, an “important contact list,” Internal Revenue Service notices, a notice of suspension from Houston’s Doctors Hospital, and a list relating to medical and hospital records.

Investigators contacted Cherilyn Lee, Jackson’s former nurse, on Wednesday as well. Lee told CNN’s Nancy Grace that they requested copies of the singer’s medical files in her possession. She said she provided the records to representatives of the coroner’s office.

Ed Chernoff, the Houston attorney Murray retained shortly after Jackson died, said detectives from the Los Angeles Police Department and agents from the federal Drug Enforcement Administration entered Murray’s northeast Houston office Wednesday morning with a search warrant.

In a written statement issued that day, Chernoff said the warrant permitted investigators to locate and take documents and other materials they believed might amount to “evidence of the offense of manslaughter.”

Members of Murray’s legal team were present while the office was searched, Chernoff said. He identified those carrying out the operation as DEA personnel, two detectives from the LAPD’s robbery-homicide division, and Houston police officers.

Chernoff said investigators finished at about 12:30 p.m. They departed with a forensic copy of the hard drive from a business computer and 21 documents. According to him, law enforcement and the Los Angeles coroner’s office had not previously asked for any of the documents that were taken.

Tammy Kidd, a spokeswoman for Chernoff’s office, said the action caught Murray’s attorneys completely off guard because communication with authorities had remained open throughout the investigation.

A day earlier, Chernoff argued that Murray should not face criminal charges, given the doctor’s detailed, minute-by-minute and item-by-item account of Jackson’s final days. He said Murray happened to be “the last doctor standing” when Jackson died and appeared to be receiving all the blame.

Chernoff said Los Angeles investigators had questioned Murray on two occasions. No third interview had been arranged, he added.

On the night after Jackson’s death, police seized Murray’s car, which had been parked at the singer’s Holmby Hills residence. Authorities returned the vehicle to Murray several days afterward.

Chernoff also said Murray was upset by news coverage that he considered both negative and frequently inaccurate. Murray now required a bodyguard around the clock, the attorney said, and was unable to maintain his medical practice or go to work because he was harassed wherever he went.

Jackson’s death was the subject of at least two investigations. The Los Angeles County coroner was awaiting toxicology findings before deciding the cause of death. At the same time, the Los Angeles Police Department, assisted by the DEA, was examining whether criminal charges might be appropriate.

A representative of the coroner’s office said the autopsy results could become public within the following week or later.

Los Angeles Police Chief William Bratton told CNN that he intended to wait until the coroner established the precise cause of Jackson’s death. He said those findings would help officials determine whether they were dealing with a homicide or an accidental overdose.

CNN’s Alan Duke, Ted Rowlands and Randi Kaye contributed to the report.

**HOUSTON, July 22, 2009** — Federal agents and Los Angeles police searched the Houston medical office of Dr. Conrad Murray on Wednesday as investigators intensified their inquiry into the death of pop star Michael Jackson.

Agents from the Drug Enforcement Administration, accompanied by LAPD detectives and Houston police, executed a warrant at Murray’s Armstrong Medical Clinic. The warrant authorized investigators to seek evidence connected to possible manslaughter, according to Murray’s attorney, Edward Chernoff.

Authorities removed prescription medications and drug-related materials, including phentermine and clonazepam, as well as medical files and other documents. Investigators also copied or seized computer records, including a forensic image of a clinic computer hard drive. An inventory released after the search listed 21 documents and other items taken from the office.

Chernoff said Murray’s legal team was surprised by the raid because the physician had been cooperating with investigators.

“The search warrant authorized law enforcement to search for and seize items, including documents, they believed constituted evidence of the offense of manslaughter,” Chernoff said in a statement. He added that Murray had provided police with information and would continue to cooperate.

Murray was with Jackson at the singer’s rented Los Angeles home when Jackson became unresponsive on June 25. The doctor attempted to revive him before paramedics arrived. Jackson was later pronounced dead at UCLA Medical Center.

Investigators have been examining medications administered to Jackson and are particularly focused on powerful sedatives and anesthetics, including propofol. Authorities have not said that propofol was recovered during Wednesday’s Houston search, and no charges have been filed.

The Los Angeles County coroner has not yet released a final cause of death, pending toxicology and other laboratory tests.

## Criminal investigation into Michael Jackson’s death

In late July 2009, the investigation into Michael Jackson’s June 25 death was increasingly centered on his personal physician, Dr. Conrad Murray, while authorities awaited toxicology results before determining an official cause of death or filing charges.

### Dr. Conrad Murray

Murray was at Jackson’s rented Los Angeles home when the singer became unresponsive and attempted to resuscitate him. Although police initially described Murray as a witness rather than a suspect, the case developed into a possible manslaughter investigation as detectives examined what medications he had given Jackson, particularly the surgical anesthetic propofol, also known by the brand name Diprivan.

Murray was interviewed by police and maintained through his attorneys that he had cooperated fully. At that stage, he had not been arrested or charged. Search-warrant language, however, showed that investigators were looking for evidence relating to the “offense of manslaughter,” indicating that his treatment of Jackson was under close scrutiny.

### Houston searches

Los Angeles police and federal Drug Enforcement Administration agents searched Murray’s Houston cardiology clinic on July 22. Authorities seized computer equipment, medical records and other material that could document prescriptions, drug purchases and Jackson’s treatment.

Two days later, investigators searched a Houston-area storage unit associated with Murray, again seeking medical records and evidence concerning medications. The raids suggested investigators were trying to reconstruct how drugs found in Jackson’s home had been obtained, who prescribed them and whether they were administered according to accepted medical standards.

The warrants and seizures did not themselves establish criminal wrongdoing; they were evidence-gathering steps in the broader death investigation.

### Cherilyn Lee’s medical files

Cherilyn Lee, a registered nurse and nutritionist who had treated Jackson earlier in 2009, provided her medical files to authorities after receiving a subpoena from the Los Angeles County coroner.

Lee said Jackson had repeatedly asked her to help him obtain Diprivan as a sleep aid. She said she refused and warned him that the drug was dangerous outside a properly equipped medical setting. Her records were potentially important because they could corroborate Jackson’s efforts to obtain propofol and establish his medical condition and treatment history before his death. There was no allegation that Lee had supplied or administered the anesthetic.

### Pending toxicology findings

The coroner had completed Jackson’s autopsy but deferred the official cause and manner of death while awaiting toxicology and other laboratory findings. Those tests were expected to identify the drugs in Jackson’s body, their concentrations and whether a combination of propofol, sedatives or other medications caused or contributed to his death.

Until those findings were completed, investigators lacked the central scientific evidence needed to decide whether Jackson’s death was accidental, the result of criminal negligence, or attributable to another cause. Consequently, no final charging decision had been made at that point.

*Later developments established that Jackson died from acute propofol intoxication, with benzodiazepines contributing. The death was ruled a homicide, and Murray was ultimately convicted of involuntary manslaughter in 2011.*

# Why investigators searched Conrad Murray’s properties after Michael Jackson’s death

**LOS ANGELES —** The searches of Dr. Conrad Murray’s home, medical offices and storage space were part of an expanding investigation into the powerful medications given to Michael Jackson before the singer’s death, with authorities looking for evidence that could support a manslaughter case.

Murray, Jackson’s personal physician, was with the pop star at his rented Los Angeles home on June 25, 2009, when Jackson stopped breathing. Investigators focused on Murray after learning that he had treated Jackson during the hours before his death and that the anesthetic propofol may have been administered inside the residence.

Propofol is normally used in hospitals and surgical facilities, where patients can be continuously monitored and emergency equipment is readily available. Its suspected use as a sleep aid in a private home raised questions about whether Jackson had been properly supervised and whether the necessary resuscitation equipment was present.

## Searches focused on medical records and drugs

Los Angeles police officers and federal drug agents searched Murray’s medical clinic in Houston, as well as properties connected to him in Las Vegas and a storage unit in the Houston area.

Search warrants indicated that investigators were seeking evidence connected to possible manslaughter, including:

- Medical and prescribing records involving Jackson  
- Documents showing what medications Murray obtained or administered  
- Records identifying pharmacies, suppliers and other doctors  
- Computers and electronic data  
- Cellphones and communications  
- Evidence involving propofol and other sedatives  

Authorities removed a computer hard drive and numerous documents from Murray’s Houston clinic. During subsequent searches, investigators carried away additional records, electronic devices and boxes of material from his Las Vegas home and office and from a Texas storage unit.

The seizures were intended to help investigators reconstruct Jackson’s final hours and determine where the drugs found in his body came from, who provided them and whether Murray’s treatment met accepted medical standards.

Investigators were also examining Jackson’s relationships with other physicians and pharmacies. Although Murray was the central figure because he was present when Jackson died, authorities sought to establish the full chain of prescriptions and medication deliveries rather than rely solely on statements from those inside the home.

## Murray’s lawyers said he was cooperating

Murray’s legal team maintained that the doctor had cooperated with authorities from the beginning and had voluntarily answered questions about Jackson’s death.

Attorney Ed Chernoff said Murray had provided investigators with relevant information and medical records. The defense expressed frustration with the searches, suggesting authorities were using highly visible raids even though Murray had not been charged at that stage.

His lawyers also disputed the suggestion that Murray intentionally harmed Jackson. They said he discovered the singer was not breathing, attempted to revive him and assisted emergency personnel. The legal team stressed that a search warrant or reference to manslaughter did not establish guilt.

Murray’s attorneys further argued that investigators needed to determine whether Jackson had access to medications from other sources and whether he could have taken additional drugs without Murray’s knowledge.

## Homicide would not necessarily mean murder

A coroner’s classification of **homicide** does not automatically mean that prosecutors believe a killing was intentional.

In death investigations, homicide generally means that another person’s actions caused or contributed to the death. If investigators concluded that Murray administered propofol and other sedatives in a medically unsafe manner, Jackson’s death could be classified as a homicide even if there were no evidence Murray intended to kill him.

Prosecutors would then separately decide whether the evidence supported a criminal charge such as involuntary manslaughter. That charge typically involves an unintentional death caused by criminal negligence or reckless conduct.

An **accidental overdose** finding would have been more likely if the evidence showed that Jackson took the fatal medication himself, received it without another person acting negligently, or died from an unintended interaction of drugs taken without criminal conduct by someone else.

The distinction depended on several questions:

- Who administered the propofol?  
- How much was given, and over what period?  
- Was Jackson properly monitored?  
- Was Murray present when Jackson stopped breathing?  
- Did Jackson take additional medication on his own?  
- Was there a delay in calling emergency services?  

Jackson’s death was ultimately ruled a **homicide** caused by acute propofol intoxication, with other sedatives contributing. Prosecutors later charged Murray with involuntary manslaughter, alleging that his treatment of Jackson was grossly negligent. Murray was convicted in 2011.
